data.title: The hidden cost of a dashboard nobody trusts
data.excerpt: A dashboard is not a data product until someone can trace its numbers back to a verified signal. Most operational reporting fails before the first chart is drawn.
data.body:
Every plant has one: a screen in the meeting room that everyone glances at and nobody uses to decide anything. It is usually not a design failure. It is a definition failure.

When a number cannot be traced to a sensor, a shift, and a calculation rule, people develop a parallel system. They keep their own spreadsheet. The official dashboard becomes decoration, and the cost shows up as repeated meetings, delayed maintenance, and arguments about whose figure is right.

Start with the decision, not the chart

The useful question is not "what data do we have?" It is "what decision changes if this number moves?" A stop-reason distribution that changes the supervisor's next action is valuable. A monthly utilisation chart that confirms what everyone already knows is expensive theatre.

  • Name the owner of each metric and the action it triggers.

  • Record the source signal, sample rate, and transformation.

  • Show data freshness and known gaps on the screen.

  • Retire metrics nobody has acted on for two quarters.

Trust is an engineering property

Traceability belongs in the data architecture. Once definitions, lineage, and freshness are treated as part of the product, the dashboard stops being a claim and starts being evidence.
